messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Another WAIC question (time series?)
parts:
After reading the Gelman, Hwang, and Vehtari paper on predictive information criteria (which is great by the way), I'm trying to think about the appropriateness of WAIC in the following (pretty common) context:  

Suppose we have J groups and T time periods, so y[t,j] is the observed value of y at time t for group j. (We also have predictors x[t,j].) I'm wondering if WAIC is appropriate in this scenario assuming that our interest in predictive accuracy is for existing groups only (i.e. we might get data for new time periods but only for the same J groups). My hunch is that this scenario requires a more complicated form of cross-validation that WAIC does not approximate, but the more I think about it the more confused I seem to become. Am I right that WAIC is not appropriate here? 
 
Thanks in advance for any advice!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
parts:
It's all a matter of formulating the likelihood.

If there are groups, the group-level parameters are
typically marginalized out.

Time series are tricky because we typically want to predict
based on past data only, not do something like full cross-validation.
I don't know how people deal with time series in WAIC.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
parts:
What I've seen done in natural language problems evaluations
is to predict/model outcome at time n given all of the
the observations from time 1 to n-1. Then you can plot the
posterior predictive log probability

log p(y[n] | y[1],...,y[n-1])

at times t[1], ..., t[N].

Rather than giving you a proper cross-validation, it gives you
something like a learning curve for the predictions.

Another thing you can do is fit all of the rest of the data

log p(y[n], y[n+1], ..., y[N] | y[1],...,y[n-1])

though if you plot you probably want to divide by (N - n + 1) to
scale everything to average prediction. It gives you a posterior
predictive cross-entropy rate estimate of the data vs. the model.

- Bob

Hi Bob, 

Regarding your first suggestion (predicting the outcome at time t conditional on the observations before t), I'm wondering what the best way is to implement something like this (using R and Stan). My first thought is to loop over the time periods in R and, for each one, run the model in Stan using the data up to that time, predicting the next outcome in generated quantities. So a very simplified version of this might be something like this:

Stan code :

# Note: I just wrote this out to be as simple as possible, so not worried about priors, optimizing code, or even if the model itself makes much sense, etc.

data {
  int<lower=1> T ; // time periods
  int<lower=1> J ; // groups
  matrix[T,J] y ; // outcome  
  matrix[T,J] x ; // predictor
  vector[J] x_next ; // predictor at next time period T+1  
}
parameters {  
  real a ;
  real b ;
  real c ;
  real<lower=0> sigma ;
}
model {
  for (j in 1:J) // loop over groups
   for (t in 2:T) // loop over time  
    y[t,j] ~ normal(a + b * y[t-1, j] + c * x[t, j], sigma) ;
}

generated quantities {
  vector[J] y_next_pred ;  
  for (j in 1:J)
    y_next_pred[j] <- normal_rng(a + b * y[T, j] + c * x_next[j], sigma) ;
}


R pseudo-ish code: 

T <- number of time periods

stan_save <- list()

stan_compile <- compile C++ code

for (t in 2:(T-1)) { # start at 2 because we need obs n-1 in the likelihood

  data_t <- list(y = y[1:t, ],  x = x[1:t, ],  x_next = x[t+1, ], J = J, T = t)

  stan_out <- stan(fit = stan_compile, data = data_t, pars = c(“y_next_pred”), whatever other arguments ... )

  stan_save[[t-1]] <- extract(stan_out)

}



Am I on the right track here? 

Thanks again for the help!

In outline, that's the only way I can think to make it work.
But I didn't understand the details of what you were doing below.

I'd have thought you'd set up a model like this:

int T;
real t[T]; // times t
int T_last;
real x[T]; // predictors
real y[T]; // outcomes

model {
head(y,T_last) ~ normal(mu,sigma);

generated quantities {
double ll;
ll <- normal_log(tail(y,T-T_last), mu, sigma);

This is a really simple model that doesn't actually have a time
series model per se, but it illustrates the general point of using
the first 1...T_last items to estimate parameters (here mu and sigma)
and then use those parameters to estimate the log density of the
rest of the data from times T_last + 1 ... T.

- Bob

There's an outcome Y measured at T equally spaced years for each of J different groups (e.g. different races, or genders, etc). There's also one or several covariates X for each of the T years and J groups. The idea is that the mean of the normal likelihood for Y[t,j] is some function of previous Y's (for simplicity we can just assume only dependence of Y[t-1,j]) as well as X[t,j], i.e. mu[t,j] = g(Y[t-1,j], X[t,j]). In the example code in my previous post I made it a simple linear function, but it could be something more complicated.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Another WAIC question (time series?)
parts:
My 2 cents: It seems as if Leave-One-Out cross-validation (which WAIC approximates) presupposes that an observation can be left out "at random", i.e. it perhaps depends on the index of the observation but the indices are exchangeable. And exchangeability does not hold with time-series data. A more general approach might be for one observation (at a time) to be considered missing, as opposed to left out. Then estimate the missing observation, along with the other unknowns, compare the posterior distribution of the missing observation to the actual data point, do that for all observations that you have, and average. In that case, it would be pretty explicit that we are talking about ability to predict a missing value among existing groups, rather than predicting a set of values for a new group. But it is not clear to me whether WAIC converges to that. So, if possible, I guess I would try to brute force the cross-validation, treating one observation at a time as missing.

Ben

OK, I see what you're doing in terms of model.

Your generated quantities block is performing a posterior
predictive simulation. What I was writing was more like
a cross-validation where you fit on earlier data and
then look at the fitted log probability function for new
data.

You could generalize to predict more than just one time
and continue the time series.

For simulation, you could also put the y_next_pred in the model and
sample them all jointly. This would only be motivated by a more
complex model --- if possible, it's much much more efficient,
both computationally per iteration and statistically in terms of
effective sample size, to do it using RNGs.
